title: India May Miss FIFA World Cup 2026 on TV as Broadcast Rights Stall
excerpt: Delhi High Court intervenes after no broadcaster secures rights, with JioStar's $20 million bid rejected by FIFA
body:
With the FIFA World Cup 2026 barely a month away, India — home to one of football's fastest-growing fan bases — still has no confirmed broadcaster for the tournament. The Delhi High Court has now stepped in, issuing notices to the Union Government and Prasar Bharati demanding answers on why 1.4 billion people might be locked out of the world's most-watched sporting event.

**The Rights Deadlock:**

The crisis stems from a collapse in commercial negotiations. FIFA initially valued India's 2026-2030 broadcasting package at USD 100 million, a figure no Indian broadcaster was willing to match. The global body eventually slashed its asking price to USD 35 million, but even that proved too steep. JioStar, the merged entity of India's two largest sports broadcasters, reportedly offered USD 20 million — a bid FIFA rejected outright.

The gap reflects a broader reckoning in Indian sports media. Despite 745.7 million fan interactions during the 2022 Qatar World Cup, football's commercial value in India still trails cricket by orders of magnitude. Broadcasters, burned by expensive rights deals that failed to deliver proportionate advertising revenue, are increasingly cautious.

**Constitutional Questions:**

Advocate Avdhesh Bairwa filed the petition citing Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Indian Constitution, arguing that access to a sporting event of national importance is a fundamental right. The plea invokes the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, which requires that events of national importance be available on free-to-air channels like Doordarshan and DD Sports. The court noted the petition's resemblance to a public interest litigation and has scheduled the next hearing for May 20 — just three weeks before the tournament kicks off on June 11.

**Why Indian-Americans Should Care:**

The broadcast blackout would hit the diaspora in unexpected ways. For millions of Indian-Americans who watch major sporting events with family back home — coordinating WhatsApp watch parties across time zones, debating group-stage upsets — the shared experience depends on both sides having access. Parents in Delhi and kids in Dallas watching the same goal at the same moment is the connective tissue of diaspora sports culture. A blackout in India severs that thread for all 104 matches running through July 19.

The situation also underscores India's peculiar position in global sports economics: massive audience, modest willingness to pay. For NRI entrepreneurs and media executives, the gap represents both a market failure and an opportunity.

**What to Watch:**

The May 20 hearing will be decisive. If the court directs Prasar Bharati to acquire rights, the government could face a bill of USD 35 million with weeks to negotiate. The alternative — India going dark during the biggest World Cup in history, with 48 teams and matches across the US, Mexico, and Canada — would be an embarrassment New Delhi can ill afford.
nri_angle: Indian-Americans who watch matches with family back home face losing the shared experience; the US-hosted tournament makes this especially relevant for the diaspora community.
